other_mijikenda: Duruma: todza (Pakia App. VI); also Swahili

teaser.en: Its seeds twist into tangles and drill into socks and skin; its stems thatch Digo houses.

summary.en: Nguji is spear grass, a tufted grass whose dark, twisted awns knot together and whose sharp seeds stick in clothing. Pakia lists it among the grasses the Digo use in house building.

about.en:
*Nguji* is a tufted perennial grass, usually knee- to waist-high, with flattened leaf sheaths and narrow leaves. Its flower spikes end in long, dark brown awns that twist together when dry, so a ripe clump looks matted and tangled.

Each seed has a sharp, hard point and a spiralling awn that coils and uncoils with moisture, screwing the seed into the ground, or into socks, wool and skin.

where.en: It grows on open grassland, bush clearings, roadsides and dry, stony slopes across the tropics, and is common on the coastal plain.

uses.en: Pakia names *Heteropogon contortus* among the grasses the Digo use for house building, alongside *Hyparrhenia* and *Cyperus exaltatus*; the stems serve as thatch. Young growth is good grazing before the seeds form.

names.en: Pakia records two Digo names, *nguji* and *todza*; *todza* is shared with Duruma and Swahili. *Todza* is also the name of blackjack (*Bidens pilosa*), another plant with clinging seeds. Pakia's name-prefix table lists both *nguji* and *todza* under blackjack, so which plant each name belongs to needs checking. In English it is spear grass or tanglehead.
